newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea June exports rise for third straight month.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea June exports rise for third straight month.

text.p: South Korea's exports rose 9.2 percent to $12.3 billion in June, marking the third straight monthly rise for 1997, provisional figures released by the trade ministry showed on Tuesday.
June May June 96
Trade balance 97.6 -613 -426
NOTE: in millions of dollars, May figures revised
Exports posted negative growth in the January through March period.
The customs-cleared trade swung to a $97.6 million surplus in June from a $426 million deficit a year earlier, the ministry said. This marks the first surplus since December 1994.
Imports gained 4.4 percent to $12.2 billion in June.
The ministry said South Korea's customs-cleared trade deficit totalled $9.36 billion in the first half of this year, up from $8.07 billion in the same 1996 period.
The monthly surplus also compared to a shortfall of $613 million in May, the figures showed.
"A rise in semiconductor exports and growth in sales of petrochemical and steel products prompted the increase in exports," the ministry said.
Semiconductor sales abroad gained 27.3 percent in June, while exports excluding computer chips rose 6.9 percent.
The ministry said the imports rose last month despite a 3.3 percent fall in May because comparable import figures for June last year were relatively low.
It said imports of capital goods posted firm growth of 21.5 percent in June on signs of an economic recovery.
However, imports of consumer materials slipped for the second consecutive month in June due to a decline in international grain prices and slowing corn imports.
The ministry said it was too early to predict a bullish trend despite the June surplus.
"Imports of capital goods could increase in the second half in line with the economic recovery," the ministry said. "Moreover, agricultural imports are likely to grow on import deregulation."
The trade ministry earlier forecast a $14 billion trade deficit this year against a $20.62 billion shortfall in 1996.
